  • Interpretation of each individual data type exchanged within this container (e.g., Opus audio data, video data, desktop sharing and input/control data).

  • Continuous monitoring of TeamTalk upgrades to detect any changes in these data streams, without the simplicity of being able to read them as text. Alternatively, and likely preferred by the TeamTalk author, TTCom could incorporate the TeamTalk SDK; but this would require

  • Separate file sets for each operating system supported by TTCom.

  • A safe way to handle authorization keys for the SDK in an open-source project.

  • Considerable TTCom author financial expense due to the cost of the SDK for this type of project.

Packet Protocol Types and Type Codes

When a client connects to and logs into a server, it must make a separate connection via UDP in order to send or receive UDP traffic. TeamTalk servers keep track of what clients support by whether this separate connection has been made. A client that connects via both TCP and UDP is said to support packet protocol 1, while a client like TTCom that only connects via TCP is said to support packet protocol 0. The TTCom WhoIs command will show the packet protocol supported by any client.

This author refers to any client that does not support UDP traffic, or in other words any client using packet protocol 0, as a “text client.” TeamTalk servers do not transmit UDP data to any client that does not support packet protocol 1. This means that text clients do not receive audio, video, or desktop data from any TeamTalk server.

Note that, due to the significantly larger amount of UDP data as compared to TCP data, it is possible to verify the presence or absence of UDP data transmission from server to client via a local Internet traffic monitor. Some Internet routers/modems offer this type of information. The Windows Task Manager also offers network throughput statistics, as does the netstat command on MacOS, Linux, and similar platforms.

An Example

Suppose a client logs into a server and joins the root channel, which contains an active voice conversation and two people sending video. The following will occur:

  • The client will connect to the server via TCP.
  • The server will send a welcome message to the client via TCP.
  • If the client plans to support UDP data (packet protocol 1), it will send a UDP initialization packet to the server; and the server will send a UDP packet back in response, establishing this separate connection.
  • The client will send a TCP login command to the server and receive text (TCP) responses indicating a successful login.
  • The server will send notification loggedin events via TCP to all other logged-in clients, so they will know that this client is now logged in. If this client made the UDP exchange, that event notification will include packetprotocol=1; otherwise, it will include packetprotocol=0.
  • The client will send a join command via TCP to join the channel.
  • The server will respond with confirmation of the join, again in TCP.
  • The server will send TCP adduser events to all other clients to notify them that this client has joined the channel.
  • If this client made the UDP exchange, the server will begin sending UDP data for all voice and video traffic in the channel to the client; otherwise, it will not.
  • If this client supports UDP data (packet protocol 1), it will begin translating the server UDP data into sound, video, etc.
TTCom Plugins

TTCom supported “triggers” for many years but began calling them “plugins” in 2024. This section and its subsections describe the plugin interface at the time of writing, updated as necessary as the interface may evolve. Changes in the plugin interface will appear as part of the TTCom revision history in this document along with other changes per public TTCom release.

Disclaimer: This TTCom author is responsible for the code that is part of TTCom itself, as released on this dlee.org website, but is not responsible for any code developed and/or used within TTCom by or from other authors. Any plugin code developed by this TTCom author is covered by the same disclaimer of liability that covers TTCom itself.

Overview

A TTCom “plugin” is a file or folder of code that TTCom runs in addition to its own code. Plugins generally add special handling of TeamTalk events, such as announcement, logging, speaking, sending push notifications, etc., when certain things happen in TeamTalk. All plugins are written in Python, although they may load other code as necessary.

Note for Windows environments: Any .pyd files required by a plugin must be created from the same Python version that is used to run TTCom itself (both the major and minor versions must match). When TTCom is run from an installed copy of Python, this works naturally. However, this requirement is especially important to remember for ttcom.exe. At this writing, ttcom.exe is built with Python 3.12; so any plugin .pyd files must also be from Python 3.12 and must be bundled with the plugin.

At this writing, all plugins should be placed under a plugins folder under the folder containing TTCom itself. This is true whether TTCom is run from source or from ttcom.exe on Windows. The very existence of files and folders in this plugins folder is enough to make TTCom use them; there is no need to register them explicitly in any other way. See the next subsection for how to make a plugin activate.

When TTCom starts or the refresh command is used, the list of successfully loaded plugins will print. Any errors encountered while trying to load a plugin will also print, and the plugin will not be activated and will not appear in the printed list.

Creating and Activating a Plugin

To create a plugin, follow these steps:

  • Create a plugins folder under the TTCom folder, if it does not already exist.
  • For simple plugins, place the code in a .py file in the plugins folder. The basename of the plugin’s code file will become the plugin’s name.
  • For more complex plugins, place the code in a subfolder under plugins, and make __init__.py contain or load the plugin’s top-level code. The folder name will become the name of the plugin. This latter option should significantly simplify management of complex plugins.
  • Note that behavior when there is a simple plugin .py file whose basename matches a plugin folder name is not defined, and this scenario is not supported.
  • Also note that the order of plugin activation is not defined and may vary among machines and operating systems. Plugins all load when TTCom starts and when the user types a refresh command at the TTCom prompt. The refresh command is therefore a fast way to load new code after editing a plugin. Accordingly though, a plugin should not assume that it will only be activated once during a run of TTCom.
Plugin Code

Import trigger_cc’s TriggerBase class so you can inherit from it. There are other common imports that may also be useful:

from trigger_cc import TriggerBase
from time import sleep
# This makes say("hello") work on MacOS and wherever a say command exists.
from mplib.mycmd import say as mycmd_say
# and for any reference to configuration options:
from conf import conf

For server srv triggers, you can define class Trigger_srv(TriggerBase). For multi-server triggers, define class Trigger(TriggerBase). (This of course can also handle server-specific triggers, such as by having __init__() check self.server.shortname against specific server shortnames.) Server-specific classes are only recommended when it is clear that the code will only ever need to apply to a single server. Trigger_srv classes are instantiated before Trigger().

In your class, include something like this:

    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        # Always include this line.
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        # Whatever event checking/actions, i.e., triggers, you need.
        # A sample "hello world" test action that prints the fired event's name.
        self.server.outputFromEvent(f"{self.event.event}")

A Trigger object is instantiated when an event fires and released when its trigger processing is completed. Since TeamTalk fires numerous events, this means that care should be taken not to consume large amounts of time from __init__ or from anything it calls, whenever possible. This becomes an issue when running programs, producing speech, etc., and even when selecting a suitable value for a time.sleep() pause. If a plugin takes a very long time, TeamTalk server timeouts may result.

Notes on printing and speaking messages:

  • Use self.server.outputFromEvent instead of print, so user choices of how to handle event output are honored. Such user choices include the silent settings for specific servers and the values of the global queueMessages and speakEvents options.
  • Use self.server.errorFromEvent for error messages.
  • If you need to produce non-error output regardless of user preferences, use self.server.output. This will print immediately however, bypassing the global queueMessages option. Its advantages over print are
    • Automatic handling of line wrapping and window width.
    • Inclusion of the shortname of the server that fired the event.
Special Notes For Plugins That Use Windows COM

Use of Windows COM from Python requires special consideration when calls come from a Python thread. Because TTCom plugins are called from threads, this TTCom author recommends the following practice. Failure to follow this practice can cause bizarre problems, such as the first four or five calls failing and the rest succeeding, according to this author’s experience in 2025. Improvements are welcome; this advice comes from this author’s work on Clisk, a Skype command-line interface, from farther back than 2010.

  • import pythoncom into your plugin.

  • Wrap COM calls, or blocks of calls, thus:

    sys.coinit_flags = 0 pythoncom.CoInitialize() # Your COM call or block of calls here. pythoncom.CoUninitialize()

  • This will ensure that the current thread is set up for Python COM calls regardless of whether any have been made from this thread already.

Resources For Plugins

Useful properties and methods given via TriggerBase and available under self in a plugin’s classes:

event

The event that just fired, as a ParmLine object. event.event is the event’s name/keyword, and event.parms is an AttrDict of the event’s parameters. (AttrDict lets you access members like nickname as either parms["nickname"] or parms.nickname, where parms.nickname actually acts like parms.get("nickname") by returning None if there is no nickname member.)

server

The TeamTalkServer object that fired the event. This provides server.users, server.info, etc. self.server.users[self.event.parms.userid] would be the record for this event’s user. (Sometimes, userid will need to be srcuserid, destuserid, etc., depending on the event.)

runCommand

A method that can execute a user-level command string as if the user typed it. This event’s server will be the “current” server at the time of the command’s execution. self.runCommand("system play beep.wav") would attempt to play beep.wav from the TTCom folder on systems that support this operation.

myIP

The IP address of this client on the server that fired this event. Warning: myIP may be None before this user’s loggedin event is completed.

See also methods in the TriggerBase class in trigger_cc.py. Examine ttapi.py classes for information on server, user, and other object types.

The following modules are preloaded into the compiled ttcom.exe file for Windows, which means that plugins may import them, or symbols from them, without incident in that environment. Users who elect to run TTCom from source on Windows will have to arrange for these modules to be available in the active Python version if the modules are needed by a plugin. These modules are not used by TTCom itself at this writing (June, 2025).

  • platform
  • ctypes
  • pywintypes
  • pythoncom
  • win32com.client
  • winsound
  • future
Known Issues

The following issues are known and may be fixed in a future version of TTCom:

General Issues

Events that print in the TTCom window can break up a command while it is being typed and can also break up the display of file transfer progress. The solution to this problem would require a full-screen interface, which though possible can complicate portability across operating systems and platforms.

Running a time-consuming command on a non-current server, using the switch command or its > equivalent, will temporarily make the target server “current.” If either the previously current server or the target have silent=1 in effect, this may affect which events are seen in the TTCom window while the command is executing. This is especially worthy of note for long file transfers started with commands like one of these:

` server paul file get war_and_peace.mp3 ~/books

jolene file send please.mp3

`

A refresh after changes to some server parameters causes a logout and login even though this is not strictly necessary. Examples of such parameters include nickname, statusMsg, and channel. While it is technically possible to fix this, it is not likely to happen for several reasons:

  • The impact of this issue in general is expected to be reasonably infrequent per TTCom user.
  • A nickname change without logout and login can be blocked by a TeamTalk server.
  • Status-changing parameters coalesce into a single command, and duplicating that calculation increases the likelihood of future bugs.
  • Changing the initial channel with a channel or chanid parameter update would not apply in practice for an account whose server-side entry includes an initial channel (initchan), so TTCom applying such a change would contradict expected TeamTalk behavior. The geolocate command only prints the first half of Canadian zip codes, stopping at the space. This is a shortcoming in the data provided by the service TTCom is using for this feature. As a result, the issue will only be fixed if either the service begins providing the full zipcode or TTCom starts using a different service.
Time Zone and Time Display Issues

TTCom’s idea of the times on certain events, such as server bans shown in a ban list, may differ from those shown by other TeamTalk clients. At this writing, a perfect method of getting this right is not known, for several reasons:

  • The TeamTalk server appears to store the time of such events, when they are entered, using the TeamTalk server machine’s idea of current time. Some servers use UTC, otherwise known as GMT; some use local time based on machine location, and still others may use local time based on server manager’s time zone, which may be nowhere physically near the machine itself; such decisions are usually up to the managers of the server machines.
  • The actual time stored by TeamTalk is a timestamp represented as the number of seconds since January 1, 1970, in whatever time zone was used when the time was saved. This timestamp does not include an indication of which time zone that was.
  • Each TeamTalk client, including TTCom, must convert such timestamps back to real times. This is typically done by adding the number of seconds in the timestamp to January 1, 1970, in the client user’s current time zone. This zone may of course be different than the one used when saving the time in the first place.
  • TTCom’s idea of “current time zone” is what Python considers the current time zone, which can depend on several factors including which Python version is installed, whether the user has defined environment variables such as TZ that affect this determination (this can cause TTCom to display a different time than shown by another client on the same computer), and how accurate is the installation’s data regarding time zones and daylight saving change information for the zone.
  • Changes in local law can, and sometimes do, alter the determination of local time arbitrarily. The most common U.S. example is a state or region changing whether it does or does not honor daylight saving time. Federal changes in when daylight saving time starts and ends have also occurred. These changes of course will cause incorrect times to display even under the best circumstances until the locally-stored time zone information is updated to reflect the new laws.
Revision History

This is the revision history of TTCom, most recent revision first:

Revision 1672, August 1, 2026
  • Users of Arch Linux and other platforms that have no release names should no longer encounter tracebacks. Thanks to Daniel Nash for discovering and reporting this issue.
  • TTCom understands two new log event flags that were added in recent TeamTalk versions:
    • streamStart: Log when a user starts a new stream.
    • logEncError: Log when a user login attempt causes an encryption error.
  • This fixes two issues:
    • A change to a new flag will show what changed instead of generating a TTCom event without indicating what happened.
    • The server info command can show when the new flags are set or unset. Note that many servers do not have one or both of these flags set at this writing (July, 2026).
  • The url and tt commands, for making a URL or .tt file for connecting to the currently connected server, will use the actual encryption state of the current connection as the value of the encrypted parameter in the server setup URL or file. The value from ttcom.conf will only be used as a fallback, such as when the server is not currently connected. Thanks to Johann for this suggestion.
  • The umsg and pmsg commands will print a warning when sending a message to a user that is not set up to see it.
  • There is a new hrsize command for reporting byte counts in a more human-readable form. This may help when designing TeamTalk configurations; for example, to determine how large a file is allowed by a max file size limit of 9999999999. By default, results are calculated using decimal calculations; e.g., 1 million bytes is 1 megabyte. Adding a b argument will cause binary calculations, where 1 megabyte is 1048576 bytes.
  • On Windows, attempts to use COM support will use late binding, to reduce the odds of confusing gencache-related error messages on the first TTCom launch.
  • Very long output blocks should no longer be truncated when TTCom is run as a Windows application from within a WSL instance. This issue mostly applies to very long lists, such as a list of downloadable files.
  • Trying to include one configuration block into more than one server configuration will no longer generate an “included more than once” error. Thanks to Simon for catching this.
  • For those who use the QueueMessages parameter and set it above 0, date/time stamps count as a message rather than appearing along with a message. For example, after the command opt QueueMessages 1, pressing Enter will display only one line at a time, even if that line happens to be a timestamp. This can sometimes improve screen readers’ ability to announce the new line correctly in a scrolling terminal window. It also facilitates rapid audio scanning through a large buffer of queued messages.
  • The code for this program now uses four spaces per indent rather than using tabs. This conforms with PEP 8, but the larger reason for this change is to improve interoperability with AI tools, linters, etc. going forward.
Revision 1638, December 20, 2025
  • TTCom will automatically figure out whether each TeamTalk server requires SSL encryption. This has several useful side effects:
    • An encrypted server that is downgraded to a plain-text server will not cause rapid connects and disconnects. It will instead connect normally but without encryption. This will happen very quickly.
    • A plain-text server that is upgraded to an encrypted server will connect correctly after a few seconds, instead of waiting for much longer, timing out, and trying again.
    • The effect of an encrypted=True ttcom.conf line for a TeamTalk server will be to make connections to that server occur within two seconds instead of more like eight.
    • If most of your server connections are encrypted, it might be prudent to add encrypted=True to the [Server Defaults] section of ttcom.conf, so that most server connections will be made more quickly.
  • Attempting to make TTCom connect to a port that hosts a non-TeamTalk service should no longer rapidly attempt reconnections. Instead, messages will print indicating what was seen and that connection attempts will stop. No more attempts will be made to reconnect to that server until the next TTCom restart, refresh command, or login command.
  • TTCom advertises to servers that it can handle TeamTalk text (TCP) protocols up through 5.14 rather than just up through 5.9. This permits TTCom to receive events on account creation and removal, if logged in as an administrator.
  • File size information printed by stats and file sizes commands now use decimal rather than binary scaling; e.g., a megabyte is one million bytes rather than 1,048,576 bytes. This change is for consistency with the scaling used in most hard drive literature and file transfer displays.
  • There are improvements in the error-handling logic for sending TeamTalk commands. If you were occasionally seeing “‘NoneType’ object has no attribute ‘send’” messages during server login or connection disruption, these should no longer appear.
  • For TTCom plugin authors, the Python version match requirement for plugins run from ttcom.exe is documented. One final apology: Revision 1473 was to have remained available for those needing older plugin support, but this revision was unknowingly lost due to a symlink accident on August 8, 2025. This revision therefore removes the links for that TTCom version from this document.
Revision 1622, August 8, 2025

Note: This is a significant update because it

  • Splits part of ttcom.conf out into a new ttcom.ini file. The file split will happen automatically when you first launch this updated TTCom revision, though the upgrade process may require manual intervention if there are errors in the configuration file such as duplicate server names.
  • Includes a complete rewrite of the code that is used to read the ttcom.conf file.
  • Significantly improves the handling of bans, though this remains an ongoing effort.
  • Alters the interfaces used by TTCom plugins, formerly called triggers.
  • Adds a more flexible way of loading plugins.
  • Includes a lot more documentation.
  • Includes numerous other updates collected over more than a year, the long release delay being due to difficulties with plugins and inter-author communications, and to this TTCom author’s having had a significant nine-month commitment to helping a friend with ALS communicate. (This TTCom author wishes to apologize for the extreme length of this delay.) A backup before upgrading TTCom is highly recommended, especially for users of TTCom plugins.

The notes for this release are broken into subsections for convenience (level 4 headings, for screen reader users wanting to jump among them). There is also a supplementary audio information file for this update, created April 2, 2024, and slightly updated January 13, 2025, for those who prefer an audio introduction to the new version. This audio file is a bit old, however, and only covers some of the major changes in TTCom. Please read these notes, even if you also play the audio file, before upgrading your TTCom instance.

Important Upgrade Considerations

There are several things to keep in mind during this update:

  • The encoding for ttcom.conf is now officially UTF-8. A byte order mark (BOM) is not required (or recommended) but will be allowed (and ignored) if found.
  • The new code for handling servers in ttcom.conf is much more careful to detect problems in server definitions. As a consequence, some issues like duplicate servers will generate errors instead of being ignored. On error, the ttcom.conf server list will not be loaded, and you will instead be asked to fix the error and either reload TTCom or use the refresh command to load the server list. Error messages will include the line number where the error was found, to help with editing.
  • Due to the better error checking at load time, the lint command is now obsolete and is removed from TTCom, along with its section in this document.
  • The only two section types allowed now in ttcom.conf are server and include. All other sections are moved to ttcom.ini.
  • There is a new ttcom_defaults.ini file. This file is currently empty but may one day have content. Do not edit or remove this file; it will be refreshed on TTCom update.
  • ttcom_default.conf is now ttcom.conf.sample. This file is not used by TTCom now but remains as a sample and possible starting point for server setup.
  • You may safely delete any local copy of ttcom_default.conf that you find.
New Documentation Sections

The following documentation sections, some with subsections, are new in this release:

  • User Account Management
  • Server and Channel Ban Management
  • The Alias Command For Making Custom Commands
  • The Box Command For Simplifying Server Address Management
  • The Flags Command For Converting Raw Flag Values To Text
  • Miscellaneous Details
  • TTCom Plugins
Plugin Documentation and Interface Changes

This TTCom update changes several items that will affect plugins, formerly called triggers. It also adds an entire section to this document on how plugins work and how to write them.

Plugins can still be loaded by creating a ttcom_triggers.py file in the TTCom folder; but this is no longer recommended or documented, and there is now a better alternative. See the new TTCom Plugins section for how to write plugins going forward. Changes in plugin interface - plugin authors, please read

Authors and maintainers of pre-existing TTCom plugins should keep the following in mind when supporting TTCom revisions before, after, or both before and after this revision:

  • The plugins folder approach only works starting after TTCom revision 1560.
  • Previous TTCom revisions considered channelid to be a synonym for chanid. This support is removed in this revision; plugins must reference chanid and not channelid. Simply change all channelid references to chanid for compatibility with both older and newer TTCom revisions. chanid has long been the correct name for this value in the TeamTalk TCP protocols.
  • Any trigger that calls a server object’s nonEmptyNickname method and passes any boolean flags should replace the flags with a single flags value composed of characters for each flag that should be True. Use character d for forceDetails, t for includeUserType, and n for noLimit. Additionally, character c will cause the user’s client name to be included after the username. As an example, the call
  • self.curServer.nonEmptyNickname(user, forceDetails=True, noLimit=True)
  • should be replaced with the call
  • self.curServer.nonEmptyNickname(user, "dn").
  • One reason for this change is to simplify any future expansion of the accepted flag list without causing newer code to stop working on older TTCom instances. If you must pass flags to this method and must also remain compatible with older TTCom revisions, it will become necessary to conditionalize the method signature based on the TTCom revision number, which can be found as an str in conf.version. To access conf, use the line
  • from conf import conf
  • Any non-server options and sections are now stored in ttcom.ini, rather than in ttcom.conf, and should be accessed via the services of the conf or configobj modules, not via iniparse which is removed from TTCom in this revision. Use only conf module calls to remain compatible with old and new TTCom versions.
  • External updates to ttcom.ini will not take effect until a refresh command is run, which will also update any servers whose definitions were changed in ttcom.conf. This is not an operational change per se since this was also true when everything was in ttcom.conf, but it is mentioned here to avoid any ambiguity.
  • Some plugins effectively create custom per-server keys in ttcom.conf. This is fine, and those that are known to this TTCom author are listed as “external” in the TTCom code as of this revision. This author would appreciate being notified of any keys being added by a plugin, so new keys can be listed. Future TTCom versions may begin producing warning messages about unrecognized keys in a server definition, to help catch typos and other similar errors.
  • conf.servers().values() returned a list before but now returns a dict. Note however that this call reads and parses the ttcom.conf file on every call, and is thus not an efficient means for obtaining both routine and custom per-server parameters. The preferred method is to use the TTComCmd.servers dict, whose keys are also shortname. One way to get this dict is from the parent property of any server object. This dict is updated only when a refresh command is run. See also the next item.
  • The loginParms key in the dict for a server contains the keys for that server from ttcom.conf. (This has been true for a very long time but was not formally documented.) For most situations, the server relevant to the firing of a trigger in one of the trigger’s methods is self.server; thus, to get the speech value for the server that fired a trigger, use self.server.loginParms['speech'].
  • This revision includes a box command that allows assignment of a “box name” to an address that is used by multiple TeamTalk servers. Both conf.servers() results and the in-memory TTComCmd.servers dict include actual addresses, not box names, for host values; so plugin writers need not worry about this change.
  • In the unlikely event that a trigger calls the toString method on any object of a BitFlags subclass, these being ChannelTypes, LogEvents, Subscriptions, and UserRights: The interface has changed so that style is the only parameter and is a string rather than an int. Translate any calls thus:
    • Styles 1, 2, and 3 become “c”, “w”, and “l”, respectively.
    • If you passed True for Optimize, add “A” to the style string and remove the second argument.
  • Any relative paths will base from the TTCom executable folder, not the plugin’s folder. A good idiom for getting the plugin’s folder, from within a plugin’s main file, is
  • os.path.abspath(os.path.dirname(__file__))
  • For a simple (non-folder) plugin, this will be the plugins folder itself. For a folder-based plugin, it will be the full path to that folder.
Changes in ban handling
  • There is a new Server and Channel Ban Management section in this document to describe the ban command in its subcommands in detail.
  • The output of the ban list command is reformatted and will include, when present, the user name of the account that created the ban. This became available starting in TeamTalk server version 5.15 (December 20, 2023).
  • The bans printed by the ban list command are ordered by increasing creation time. This may also be the default order returned by TeamTalk servers for server bans, but this sorting order is now coded into TTCom to ensure consistency and also to sort correctly when channel bans are also listed (see below).
  • The ban add command has a new -a or --address option that allows banning of an IP address, subnet, or pattern regardless of who is currently logged in. Warning: This feature is experimental, subject to change, and may or may not work as expected based on TeamTalk server version. This feature should not be used against TeamTalk servers older than 5.13 and has mostly been tested on server versions 5.15 and later. The TTCom support for adding bans of this type is being designed to work around various apparent issues in TeamTalk server handling of subnet and pattern bans. Example: ban add -a 192.168.55.
  • ban delete will display matching bans even when there is only one match.
  • The ban list command has some new options:
  • -a or --all
  • List all bans, which means server bans as usual, plus any bans found in any channels on the server. Warning: Depending on the number of channels on the server, this may take some time and may fail with flood protection errors. This TTCom author has submitted a TeamTalk enhancement request to permit a much more efficient means of retrieving all channel bans at once.
  • -C or --channel
  • List all channel bans but do not list server bans. The warning for the previous option also applies to this one. The -C short option is capitalized because -c has long been used already to return a ban count instead of a ban list.
  • -s order or --sort=order
  • Change the sort order of the printed ban list. See the new Server and Channel Ban Management section in this document for details.
Other command additions and updates
  • The alias command is now fully functional and may be used to create custom commands.
  • There is a new flags command for printing the enabled values of flags, given a flag type and value. This command is mostly for TeamTalk server box administrators who want to understand values in a TeamTalk server’s XML configuration file.
  • There is a new box command with subcommands for managing a set of hostname aliases. The point of this is to simplify the updates required when a whole set of TeamTalk servers migrates to a new Internet service provider, by allowing host lines to refer to a box (machine or VM running TeamTalk servers) by a custom name. The address of that box can then be changed in one place to cause all of those TeamTalk servers to use the new location.
  • If you try to use the join channel to join a passworded channel without giving a password, TTCom will prompt for the password. This avoids quoting problems, keeps the password from printing on screen, and keeps the password out of the TTCom command history.
  • Several commands that show TeamTalk timestamps, such as for accounts, bans, and file uploads, print invalid timestamps as “Invalid timestamp” and a number, which is the raw value for the field. This can happen when a time value is never initialized. This is not a bug or error; it simply means there is no correct value for the field, and TTCom just shows what is stored there.
  • WhoIs includes better-formatted last-login and account-last-modified time when available.
  • Bans, uploads, and accounts may sort better when sorted by time values.
  • The account list command includes a “Last Used” column showing the last login time of each account, on servers that support this field.
  • The account list command supports a -s or --sort flag to specify how to sort accounts.
  • This document finally includes a full User Account Management section documenting this command and all of its subcommands.
  • The queueMessages option can be used to prevent TTCom from printing event messages until you press Enter. Typing the command opt queue 1 will make each Enter with no command cause one message to print. Using opt queue 2 will make two messages print, etc. This will keep incoming events from appearing while you are trying to type a chat message, for example. Use opt queue 0 to return to the default behavior, where all messages print immediately as they arrive.
  • The speakEvents option can be used on non-Mac platforms if a say command exists on the path. The say command must take the text to speak on its standard input and must speak it by some means before exiting. This is also how the native say command works on MacOS. Alternatives for implementing this command
    • On Linux, a say command can be created using a speech engine package such as RHVoice or ESpeak (apt install rhvoice or apt install espeak), or by using the Speech Dispatcher where available (Debian for instance). An example of such a say command script:
    • ` #! /bin/sh
    • # Say - speak what is sent to stdin and exit.
    • # Uncomment one line below that will work on your system.
    • # See the relevant documentation for descriptions of options, and to assist in editing commands to taste.

    • # spd-say -w -e
    • # espeak -s140 -g4 -v en-us
    • # RHVoice-test -i - -r 75 -p BDL `
    • This can also be done under WSL on Windows, provided that either WSL sound works or the wrapper includes a means to send sound into a native Windows device or application.
    • On native Windows, a say wrapper can be written that uses the JAWS FSAPI or the equivalent NVDA COM interface.
  • Given this setup, typing option speakEvents 1 makes TTCom try to speak all events that print in the TTCom window.
  • TTCom can be run with a single command via a new -c option. Place the command to run after the -c option. Do not place the command in quotes. TTCom will not connect to servers when invoked in this manner, and it is an error to list servers when using this option. Examples:
  • ` # Define an alias on the fly.
  • ttcom -c alias mv move
  • # Look up an IP address (but use one that can actually be found).
  • ttcom -c geo 192.168.1.1
  • `
Other interface changes
  • If ttcom.conf does not exist on TTCom startup, TTCom will run instead of exiting but will warn of the file’s absence.
  • Raw IPv6 addresses are now permitted as hostnames in ttcom.conf. Notably, this includes ::1, the IPv6 equivalent to the IPv4 127.0.0.1 localhost address.
  • On startup and after any refresh command, the current server will become the last server that tries to log in, rather than the last server defined or refreshed.
  • EOF from a terminal will not exit this application unless received three times in a row. On Linux, this prevents a single accidental Ctrl+D from exiting and logging out of all connected servers.
  • TTCom will include its operating system type in its client name like the regular TeamTalk clients do, and more specifically than Python usually does. Elements that may appear include
    • “Windows,” “Linux,” “Cygwin,” or “MacOS” for basic operating system type, with other items following this.
    • Further refinements where possible; e.g., “Windows 11 Professional,” “Linux Debian Bookworm,” “MacOS Monterey.”
    • “WSL” or “WSL1” or “WSL2” for Windows Subsystem for Linux.
    • Identification of other virtulization technologies that contain or share with this one.
  • Full examples include “Linux Debian bookworm in kvm,” “Linux Ubuntu Noble in vmware,” and “Linux AlmaLinux Cerulean in microsoft.”
  • Various user selection lists will include each candidate user’s client name along with the nickname and username.
  • The stats command, which requires admin rights, prints file transfer statistics after rather than before the totals. This is because TeamTalk does not include file transfer byte counts in the totals.
  • Server update events will not print changes to the message of the day (motd) that result only from changes in server-side variables that are included, such as user count on the server. If the message is actually changed, the resulting motd_raw change will still be reported. This change in behavior prevents other changes, such as a user timeout adjustment, from also printing old and new copies of the motd when it did not substantively change.
  • Both the process and documentation for setting up BearWare web logins are improved a bit.
Bug fixes
  • The url and tt commands include ports when the current user does not have server property update rights.
  • The server password field in .tt files is no longer generated, as this field has not been supported by TeamTalk itself for several years.
  • The geolocate command should accept IPv6 socket addresses for IPv4 connections, e.g., addresses starting with “::ffff:,” in more circumstances.
  • Fixed the long delay on TTCom startup caused by servers that deny login via ban or invalid account. Of course there will still be a delay for servers that fail to connect at all, because TTCom must wait a while to see if the connection can succeed.
  • Servers that deny login will show with state loginError/connected instead of just connected. This is considered a bug fix because this behavior was originally intended.
  • This update includes another attempt to prevent an occasional issue where a refresh causes an extra instance of a changed server to remain logged in.
  • Fixed a bug that could cause a TypeError on a command like alias x when ttcom.ini doesn’t even contain a section for aliases yet. This issue was never reported but was proven possible.
  • Fixed a small but long-standing bug that could cause the message “Output collection aborted by server connection interruption” to print after certain command sequences. The message was harmless but also unnecessary.
  • The rel command output format is improved when a release note block contains paragraph tags.
  • A minor bug is fixed throughout TTCom that could have caused small problems on system time change. The following should work better when daylight saving or other changes modify the system clock:
    • The printing of time stamps whenever an event occurs and no timestamp has printed in the last two minutes.
    • The last-status-change times on a whoIs command.
    • The determination of when to send the next ping to a server.
Revision 1473, January 18, 2024

This is the last revision that supports the unified ttcom.conf file format, before the ttcom.ini split.

Changes in this revision:

  • When the name of a channel changes, TTCom will print the update but will no longer also print the full old and new channel paths, as this tends to look redundant.
  • The version command allows multiselection when more than one user matches the given argument. This feature was requested a while ago by Simon Jaeger.
  • The url command no longer adds encrypted=false; the encrypted parameter is only needed when it is true.
  • TTCom will no longer print typing indicators when regular client users are typing private messages, because of how much noise this tends to generate during a private message conversation. TTCom private messaging with the pmsg command still works.
  • The stats command prints its results in a much more friendly manner:
    • All fields are given better names.
    • The data transfer statistics are printed in a tabular format with human-friendly units for byte counts.
    • The server uptime is given as days + hours:minutes:seconds instead of a huge millisecond count.
  • Note that the stats command is only available to server administrators; this is a requirement enforced by TeamTalk servers.
  • Fixed an error that could cause an old server connection to remain when the configuration for the server changes to a new host address and a refresh command is issued.
  • Smartened automatic ping handling to hang onto a server when its usertimeout is shortened substantially during an active session.
  • Fixed an AttributeError on geo -v when the address lookup fails.
  • Fixed the geo command to work on an IPv6 address even from a machine that doesn’t support them. Inspired by an old Mac. 31 older revisions back through September 7, 2014
Revision 1454, November 16, 2023

Changes to commands and their responses:

  • WhoIs prints “Not connected” instead of an error if asked for info from a disconnected server.
  • Changed what happens if the geolocate command is used without arguments: Previously, this looked up the current user’s IP address. Now, it looks up the IP address of the current TeamTalk server, which can be useful in diagnosing connectivity problems such as excessive lag times. If the server is currently connected, the address of the connection is used. If it is not, TTCom looks up the server’s hostname. This can result in more than one address, such as when a server supports both IPv4 and IPv6 connections. In this case, address information will print for all returned addresses, in the order returned by the Python socket.getaddrinfo() call.
  • Fixed the -m (include me) flag on the allSummary command doing nothing. Thanks to Christopher Duffley for spotting this.
  • Updated the account list and channel list commands:
    • The -l flag for getting a long listing is changed to -v, for verbose.
    • The -e flag for requesting everything including empty fields is removed; specify -v twice, or just type -vv.
    • account list -vv will show “Note: None” for an account that has no note.
    • Similarly, channel list -vv will show “Topic: None” for a channel that has no topic.
    • account list -v or -vv will include one-word descriptions of user rights alongside the hex value of the field. When more flags are set than unset, “all but” and the unset ones print, instead of a long list of set ones. The results “all” and “none” print for cases when all or no flags are set as well. Other changes and fixes:
  • The server version that prints on a successful login is no longer truncated to a length of three characters.
  • In user rights discussions, changed terminology in this document for what was “desktop control” to “input.” This is actually consistent with language found in the TeamTalk code itself.
  • Changed the single-letter flag for the desktop input user right from “C” to “I.”
  • Changed the single-letter subscription and intercept flags for desktop input/control from “x” and “X” to “i” and “I” and the one-word codes from “control” and “iControl” to “input” and “iInput.”
  • Added support for two new user rights: permission to send private messages and permission to send channel messages. The single-letter codes used for these are “P” and “C” and the single-word codes are “PM” and “CM.” These were added to TeamTalk itself in version 5.15. As these rights are enabled by necessity in older TeamTalk versions, TTCom presents them as enabled for server versions older than 5.15.
  • Filled in the missing user right for status lock, with single letter “T” and single-word code “statusLock.”
  • Changed the single-letter code for nickLocked from “n” to a capitalized “N.”
Revision 1437, September 26, 2023
  • The Windows ttcom.exe executable is now compiled with Python 3.11 instead of Python 3.7, is distributed in its own ttcom_win.zip file instead of being part of the main ttcom.zip file along with the TTCom source code, and is no longer compacted into a single .exe file. (As a side effect, non-Windows users may now enjoy a much smaller ttcom.zip download size.) There will now be several files and folders extracted when ttcom_win.zip is expanded. This change may increase TTCom’s loading speed on Windows. This change was motivated, however, by difficulties with single-executable Python programs being routinely and inaccurately flagged by antivirus software, including Windows Defender, as threats. Details on this issue for anyone curious
  • Upon the upgrade to Python 3.11 and a current Pyinstaller version, Windows Defender began claiming that ttcom.exe contained a trojan horse. Research on this surprise immediately indicated that this problem has become very common for single-file Windows executables that are compiled from Python and a few other more rapid-development languages. This author chose to work around this problem by distributing the Windows executable as a file set instead of as a single file, rather than reverting to older Python and/or Pyinstaller versions. At this writing, it appeared as though a Pyinstaller 4.x version would otherwise have been required, though current versions are 5.x.
  • There is a new geolocate command which looks up freely available location and related information about an IP address. The initial code for this feature was contributed by Ivan Soto and uses ip-api.com to obtain its information.
  • The output of server info is improved:
    • If the server is not connected, “Not connected” will appear instead of empty results.
    • Zeros and other empty values do not print. This minimizes, for example, the output for connected but not logged-in servers. Beware, though, that this may make some expected values disappear; for example nothing will print for autosave when it is 0.
    • The raw motd value is properly formatted instead of printing “” where a new line should begin. In the unlikely event you really need the unformatted value, you can type this command to get it:
    • !app.curServer.info.motdraw
    • Note also that the motd command is the proper way to get the message of the day with any server-side variables translated into their values.
    • Any fields added in future TeamTalk server versions should print automatically below the preformatted material, so that such fields can be seen before they are properly incorporated into the output format.
  • Typing help followed by both a command and a subcommand, e.g., help account list, is allowed and will print whatever help is directly available for that subcommand. At this time though, most of this type of help will simply advise you to type the command, the subcommand, and -h for more information.
  • The whoIs command, when typed without arguments to retrieve information on the current user, avoids printing the current user’s password for TeamTalk servers that send it as part of the accepted event that is sent during the login sequence. TeamTalk servers do not send passwords for other users, so this only affects queries about yourself.
  • When the LogEvents value for a server changes, the change is shown as the added and/or removed flags rather than as the old and new decimal values of the field, which is not easy for most people to interpret.
  • Attempting to issue a command such as ping to a server that is not connected will produce the message, “OSError: Not connected,” instead of the far less explanatory, “AttributeError: ‘NoneType’ object has no attribute ‘send’.”
  • Ping timeouts no longer produce an extra IndexError message.
  • Some code is updated better to conform to expectations in newer Python versions. There are also a few code reorganizations.
  • Those installing onto Linux, MacOS, or similar may notice that a number of files that had unnecessary execute permissions no longer have this. This gratuitous assignment of execute permissions was a side effect of this author’s build environment, which was a mixture of Windows and WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux). Details for the unusually curious (like me):
  • The build environment was housed in a native Windows folder, but most of the build tools ran under WSL. Of course a glaring exception was the pyinstaller tool, which ran in Windows to make the Windows ttcom.exe file. Difficulties with running Windows utilities against WSL files delayed migration of the build environment into a WSL file folder. This is the change that permitted this update’s fix to file permissions.
  • ttcom_default.conf no longer says that TTCom is unable to log into public servers, calls them “official” servers now since “public” servers are no longer a thing in TeamTalk, and demonstrates a web login as is required by the public US server.
  • By popular vote, old history entries in this document section are now hidden inside a details tag that may be expanded to show them. Among the benefits of this, heading count is reduced and text searches won’t match very old material.
Revision 1406, June 29, 2023
  • Filtering various account, ban, and channel commands against a field that does not always exist works now instead of producing a KeyError. An example command that works now but did not before is account list !note="", which lists all accounts that have a non-empty note field.
  • The allSummarize command is renamed to allSummary, for consistency with the summary and shortSummary commands.
  • This client’s channel join and leave events are printed even when silent=2. This was inspired by cases of silent=2 causing TTCom users to be unaware that other users had moved them into or among channels without asking permission.
  • The output from the stats command is printed even when silent=2 or higher is in effect for the current server. This and the previous item are actually part of the next change.
  • The following event message types print entirely regardless of the effective silent= value in ttcom.conf:
    • Error messages from the TeamTalk server.
    • Channel joins and leaves for this user.
    • Kicks of this user from channel or server.
    • Server statistics that result from the user typing a stats command.
    • TTCom-generated asynchronous output.
  • The account list command works against TeamTalk 5.13 servers instead of producing an AttributeError. TeamTalk 5.13 servers do not send a value for the note field when it is empty, and TTCom was expecting a valid but empty value instead.
  • The account list command also includes a Last Modified column in its default output format. Beware, though, that some servers, especially older ones and servers that were set up long ago, will send bogus dates for this field, commonly dates from 1969 or 1970.
  • The summary command allows a -m flag to make results include “me” (the current user, or self). Use the help summary_flags command for details on this and the other available flags. This new flag is intended to make finding oneself and other participants in the same channel easier, which is in turn useful for those who often join a channel and use the cmsg command to text among channel participants. The allSummary and shortSummary commands also support this flag, though this may well be less useful.
  • Some command output, and the output for help summary_flags, should be improved a bit, such as by minimizing the number of times a word is split between lines. This may still happen when graphical characters appear in a line.
  • A code function that accidentally became a user command, SendMessage, is no longer a user command. This is the code that is used to send messages with the cmsg, umsg, and broadcast commands. Attempting to use the erroneous SendMessage command directly would have caused an error.
Revision 1393, March 15, 2023
  • There is a new rel command for printing the release notes for all updates that have not already been installed. The material printed by this command comes directly from the Revision History section of this document’s online version. The formatting may be less visually appealing than in a web browser however, due to limitations of Windows console output. For those who like to live on the edge, rel -b will check for and print release notes for beta revisions instead of releases.
  • There are two new commands for summarizing what files have been uploaded to the server: file counts and file sizes. These are mostly useful for server administrators; for non-admins, they are limited to the current channel.
  • The file subcommands get, check, and delete have a -o option for limiting considered files to those owned by specific users. See the new Specifying File Owners section for details on how to select file owners.
  • The account list, ban list, and channel list subcommands now have a -c option for showing only a count rather than a list. Filtering is supported for each command when counting just as when listing; e.g., account list -c -a and channel list -c !type=1 are permitted.
  • The channel command has a new flags subcommand that allows viewing and setting of various flags on a channel. Type channel flags -h in TTCom for help on this command.
  • Several commands print “You are not in a channel” instead of a Python error message when executed while the current server is not connected.
  • File send allows admins to send to channels without first joining them. This change is made in concert with TeamTalk itself officially supporting such admin behavior in official clients.
  • Fixed an error on file deletion that printed an AttributeError message after deleting a file.
  • Fixed a few formatting problems in help selection and errtrace output.
Revision 1372, November 24, 2022

Significant changes in event and trigger handling:

  • TTCom will now print the following event types for all servers regardless of the silent value for each server (but see below for a new silent=3 option)::

    • Broadcasts, channel messages, user messages, TTCom private messages, and typing notifications.
    • Server connect and disconnect messages.
    • Kicks from a server or channel.
    • Error messages sent by a server, such as account login failures, bans, etc.
    • Server updates, such as a change in the message of the day (motd).

  • This list of notification types is chosen to reflect those notifications that most users don’t want to miss. Server updates are included in this list so that very long-held TTCom connections to a TeamTalk server will still provide notifications of server policy updates. If you really need a server to be quiet, use silent=3. Note that this change will likely make trigger users want to remove any triggers specifically designed to print these events or messages. Sound-generating triggers for these may of course remain useful.

  • Date and time will print above event output when no such stamp has printed in the last two minutes. For anyone who remembers my Clisk (Command Line Interface for Skype) utility, now sadly defunct along with the Skype API it required, this behavior is taken directly from that utility.

  • All message types are reformatted to make them briefer and, as it happens, more like Internet Relay Chat (IRC) messages. See the Text Messaging In TTCom section for examples of how they will now look.

  • Trigger matches no longer print; triggers should manage their own output. This affects triggers that are written in the ttcom.conf file. An example that printed previously but no longer will: Given a trigger like this in ttcom.conf:

    match msg1.matchOnType=messagedeliver type=1 action msg1.sound=play msg1.wav

  • TTCom previously printed this on a trigger match:

    [simon] messagedeliver triggers msg1 matchOnType

  • where “simon” is the shortname for the triggering server, “messagedeliver” is the TeamTalk event name causing the trigger, “msg1” is the trigger name, and “matchOnType” is the name of the match criterion for the trigger that actually matched and caused it to fire. Trivia: This TTCom author simply forgot to remove that for a very long time, having intended it as a debugging aid. Other significantly visible and/or impactful changes:

  • When TTCom is in a channel on the current server, the prompt includes the full channel path, not just the innermost channel name. As a side effect, the root channel shows as “/” rather than not showing at all.

  • Server names in TTCom event output are now followed by a space and a dash instead of being surrounded by square brackets. This is to improve reading speed for those who use synthetic speech and have punctuation announced.

  • The perhaps infamous “j” bit in subscriptions, such as are reported by whoIs, is now “t,” for typing notification subscription. (I only figured out the purpose of this bit on November 16, 2022.)

  • As a side effect of the above change, TTCom can now unsubscribe from typing notifications from an official TeamTalk client to avoid a lot of notifications in a long or busy chat;. e.g.,

    sub dlee -t

  • Note though that unsubscribing from “typing notifications” for another TTCom user will also prevent you from receiving any messages sent by that user via the pmsg command.

  • This document is updated to reflect new discoveries regarding TeamTalk server processing of typing notifications and TTCom custom messages. These updates notably include the addition of a Technical Details On TTCom Private Messaging section.

  • The intercept command is removed, and the subscribe command is significantly rewritten and supports management of intercepts along with subscriptions. Use the command help subscribe for details. Notable among the changes is the use of single-letter flags rather than words for subscription and intercept flags. Other changes and fixes:

  • Rapid event output lines should no longer sometimes intermingle in the output onto the same line. This is especially noticeable during TTCom startup when many server connections occur simultaneously.

  • Including non-standard characters in the ttcom.conf configuration file, such as emojis in a nickname field, caused errors on TTCom launch on Windows (not WSL). This has been fixed via a TTCom-specific modification to the included IniParse library. The ttcom.conf file is now assumed to use UTF-8 character encoding regardless of operating system.

  • There is a new beep command that sends a bell character to the TTCom output. This may be useful for those who run TTCom in remote ssh sessions and use triggers for alerts for certain events. Another perhaps better alternative, though, is to create a play command on the remote machine’s PATH, such as

    #! /bin/sh echo -n >&2 “\07”

  • This would have the effect of making TTCom produce one beep for every sound or rapidly-generated group of sounds, whereas using the beep command in a trigger will generate one beep per triggering event, even when they occur rapidly.

  • A couple of calls to the Python eval function are replaced with more efficient techniques.

  • A number of old exception-handling cases are hardened against untimely typing of Ctrl+C.

  • The gzip module is no longer imported as it is not being used.

  • Irregular termination of play commands executed from a trigger, which some users use to play sounds on certain events, should no longer cause all future TTCom sound file playing to stop working until the next TTCom restart. This problem may still not be fully fixed, however.

Revision 1330, August 2, 2022

Major updates:

  • The server command for switching servers or running a command against a non-current server is changed to switch, to make room for commands to query and manipulate server properties and/or TTCom configurations for servers. The > shortcut still works as before, by being translated to switch.
  • There is a new pmsg command for sending more private text messages among TTCom clients. Previously, this was accomplished with UMsg -i.
  • The UMsg command’s -i option is removed, as the above command replaces it.
  • A new server info command prints all server property information for the current server.
  • TTCom can now send messages longer than 512 characters, as other TeamTalk 5.9+ clients can. How they appear on the receiving end will of course depend on the receiving client: For 5.9 and later clients, they will appear as a single message. On older clients, they will appear as multiple messages. At this time, TTCom will show them as multiple messages.
  • The output of bit flags in the following commands is improved, so that when more flags are set than unset, “all but” and the unset ones print, instead of a long list of set ones. The results “all” and “none” print for cases when all or no flags are set as well.
    • server info, for the event logging value.
    • account list -r (list accounts by user rights), for user rights values.
    • channel list with -l or -e, for channel type values.
    • whoIs, for the user rights value. Minor updates and bug fixes:
  • If TTCom is in a channel, the prompt will include the final component of the channel name - i.e., the name of the channel or subchannel but not the entire path to it from the root of the channel tree.
  • The shortSummary command abbreviates lists of users on a server when several share the same name, by placing a count and an “x” in front of the duplicated name. This feature was inspired by an Internet radio station server on which an instance of the station’s stream typically appeared in several channels at once.
  • The url command includes the channel password when appropriate. Due to a bug, this was being omitted.
  • The url command works when channel names and/or passwords contain spaces or other special characters. Note though that TeamTalk client versions prior to 5.7.1 or so will still not process these URLs correctly.
  • File sending, downloading, and deleting also work on file names containing special characters.
  • The lint command for reporting problems and anomalies in ttcom.conf is updated:
    • bearwareid sections are understood.
    • nickLimit no longer causes a warning.
    • serverpassword causes a warning, as it has been obsolete since the arrival of TeamTalk 5.0.
  • There is improvement in the language used to indicate how much time has passed between the most recent status change and the current one.
  • Fixed a KeyError that was seen twice over the last three years in the summary command. The error occurred when a user was in a channel whose name could not be retrieved. Now when this occurs, TTCom will show the channel with a name like “”, where “10” is the channel id in the TeamTalk TCP protocol. Thanks to Chris Duffley for a precise error report demonstrating this issue.
Revision 1305, January 2, 2022
  • The account list, account delete, and account users commands accept a -n argument to restrict the results to “normal” (non admin, non disabled) accounts. Specifying more than one of -a, -d, and -n for any of these commands will also generate a SyntaxError instead of resulting in no matching accounts.
  • The account users command allows the -d argument to restrict to disabled accounts, though this should never produce any results since disabled accounts do not allow login.
  • Setting a blank note field with the account mod command with note="" or just note= works as expected.
  • Errors occurring during the execution of a trigger will no longer cause subsequent trigger actions to be skipped.
  • The support for playing sounds from a trigger is reorganized, with a few results:
    • Sounds may be very slightly delayed so that they can be more efficiently collected into fewer SoX commands.
    • There is support for playing sounds using SoX effects without using sound files. An example ttcom.conf trigger for making a server connection sound using a SoX effect:
    • ` match connected.connected=connected
    • action connected.sound=play synth 0.1 exp 330-550 vol .2 `
    • Beware that synth sounds are natively full volume, so adding a vol effect to such requests is very useful.
  • Errors during locale setup print but no longer cause TTCom to abort. This issue was only reported by one user in the several years during which TTCom has honored locale settings.
  • A few URLs in this document are updated to reflect more accurately the current locations of TTCom beta and release files. This includes fixing the download link in the beta version of this document so that it downloads the beta rather than the release version of TTCom.
Revision 1288, November 23, 2021
  • This document includes a new “Summarizing Who Is Where On Servers” section to document the commands used for summarizing where users are.
  • The summary, allSummarize, and shortSummary commands support a new set of summary flags that determine which clients/users to include in the output.
  • Typing help summary_flags in TTCom itself provides information on how the new summary flags work.
  • The default behavior of the shortSummary command is changed to omit text clients even when they are in a channel. To get the original behavior of including these clients, add a -c flag, which means include everyone in a channel regardless of client type.
  • The whoIs command prints the “modifiedTime” value as a date and time instead of as a (usually large) integer. For date/time values before or during 2004 (which predates TeamTalk), the raw integer value is also shown. The whoIs command only shows this field when run against your own TTCom instance.
  • Documented the difficulties with determining how to display times of TeamTalk events.
  • Fixed a bug that would cause a “KeyError: username” error message and traceback on an attempt to log in via the anonymous account into a professional TeamTalk server.
  • Fixed the printing of “\r” in typing indicator messages produced by clients that send them, such as the Qt client for MacOS and Windows.
  • Stopped shortening nicknames in the following circumstances even when the nickLimit option has been set by the user:
    • User nickname matching for all commands that include this feature.
    • The output of the version command when applied to a user.
    • The result of the nickname command when used to check your own nickname.
    • The ban add command’s user selection list.
    • The op command.
Revision 1277, October 23, 2021
  • CMsg, UMsg, and Broadcast commands should handle quotes more consistently and no longer produce syntax errors on some lines containing quotes.
  • The above messaging commands also support sending multi-line messages. To do this, don’t specify any message text with the command. TTCom will prompt you to enter the text to send, ending with a dot (.) on its own line.
  • Multiline messages of any type print properly instead of showing \n in place of line endings.
  • The ban command supports a count subcommand, for indicating how many bans, or how many bans matching a filter, exist on a server.
  • The prefix system ignores blank lines, so that pressing Enter at a prompt does not cause error messages.
  • The ping command includes the number of milliseconds between ping and server response. This can be useful for measuring lag time between client and server.
  • The internal timing of server pings is tuned to improve TTCom’s ability to hang on to connections during a rough moment of Internet connectivity. Up to now, TTCom actually pinged servers far less often than did official TeamTalk clients. This will likely still be the case for high server usertimeout values; but for the normal value of 60 seconds, TTCom now pings every 30 seconds like other clients do.
  • Trigger failure errors include one-line tracebacks similar to what the errTrace command produces for other errors.
Revision 1262, September 15, 2021
  • There is support for logging into TeamTalk servers via the BearWare.dk web authentication system. This makes it possible to use TTCom with some public and professional TeamTalk servers that require this type of login.
  • There are new man and www commands for launching TTCom’s user guide or the TeamTalk home page in the default browser.
  • The TTCom command prompt includes the name of the currently selected server when there is one (and there almost always is one).
  • There is a prefix command that may be useful when exchanging text messages.
  • The option command supports a new nickLimit option, the numeric value of which will limit the length of nicknames printed by several commands. Nicknames longer than this will be cut short and end with an ellipsis. Unless this option is set to an integer value, full nicknames will always print. This feature was inspired by a small band of TeamTalkers who carried around nicknames over 300 characters long.
  • There is a new clTypes command that lists how many people are using each client type across all logged-in servers. The purpose of this command is to help track the progress of adoption of the TeamTalk Qt client by long-time users of the Windows TeamTalk Classic client for accessibility.
  • File transfer commands display and sort by the file upload time added in TeamTalk 5.8.1 when available.
  • The -e option to the account list command formats the value of the modifiedtime parameter, added in TeamTalk 5.8.1, as a date/time value instead of a long number.
  • This document includes a new section documenting, in some technical detail, the nature of TeamTalk communication and what TTCom does and does not support. There are also a few minor mechanical fixes to the documentation.
Revision 1234, July 31, 2021

This update’s release notes are divided into sections because of the number of changes.

Changes to the file management commands:

  • The file list and file delete commands print files in approximate upload time order rather than in alphabetical order.

  • When used from a non-admin account, the file delete command will only list files belonging to the current user’s account. This is because TeamTalk servers will not allow a non-admin to delete a file uploaded under a different account, and allowing this command to attempt to do so would only cause error messages.

  • There is a new file check command for finding records for files whose data is no longer available on the server. This subcommand was inspired by a series of events over a few months in which a wayward server administrator deleted the root channel and then got the channels restored by arranging for the restoration of the TeamTalk server configuration XML file, which restored hundreds of file records for files that were actually removed from the server. The new subcommand provides means to remove all file records for files that no longer exist. Other command changes and additions:

  • ban del works again; not sure when this broke.

  • account list -r is reformatted and includes the number of users in each list as well as a brief list of the rights themselves along with the hex rights values already printed. The total number of accounts is also included.

  • The account command has a new users subcommand that lists currently logged-in users organized by the accounts they are using. The subcommand accepts the -a flag to include only admin accounts, allows containment filtering on username, and allows "" to match the anonymous account. This subcommand does not require admin rights because it does not need to access the list of available accounts; it simply uses the list of logged-in users to derive the list of accounts shown.

  • The channel type printed by the channel list command is now printed in hex instead of decimal and includes a list of the type flags. The one-word-per-flag format is used when -l is specified; otherwise, the single-letter flag format is used. Documentation and miscellaneous updates:

  • TTCom server setup is documented.

  • There is a new “Making TTCom Join a Channel On Login” section documenting how to make TTCom join a channel on login. This was previously only documented in these release notes.

  • TTCom now allows the setting of gender identification and a status message; see the section on setting defaults for details.

  • When TTCom displays gender identification, it will use m for male, f for female, and n for TeamTalk’s third option. Previously, the designations printed as male, female, and neutral; this change is to permit wider end-user interpretation; e.g., man vs male, nonbinary or neither vs neutral.

  • When a user’s status changes from Away to Question and Away at the same time, TTCom correctly indicates the new Question mode. Previously, it printed “stat3” instead, because it is not normally possible to set both modes in the Classic client at the same time. The Qt client does allow this.

  • When logging in to a server, TTCom sends a protocol identifier like other TeamTalk clients do. Currently that identifier is “5.8.”

  • This guide includes a table of channel type flags, and there are other minor documentation updates.

  • TTCom can support arbitrary terminal widths instead of assuming the very old safe minimum of 79 characters. This means that if your terminal/console window is wider, TTCom will now more often fill it instead of leaving the right side unused.

  • Removed a bit of old code for support of Windows XP.

  • Observant MacOS and Linux users may notice that all files now have the execute (x) permission bit set. This is a harmless, if unusual, side effect of this author’s having to migrate all development projects in June, 2021, from Cygwin to the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL) without also moving the files themselves into a native Linux file space.

Revision 1192, March 25, 2021

Note: This release was initially missing two files required for running TTCom from source. This was corrected on April 9, 2021, without a revision or code change.

  • The tt command for creating .tt files allows constructs like ~, ~username, and $HOME as part of file paths.
  • The kick command allows a -c option for kicking from channel instead of server. This duplicates the cKick command but in a way that more easily supports command dictation in place of typing.
  • Being kicked from a channel produces the correct “kicked from channel” announcement instead of saying “kicked from server,” and no longer causes a “manual login” condition that might otherwise have made the next Internet disruption result in TTCom failing to reconnect.
  • The WhoIs command, rather than printing simple integers, prints subscriptions as both hexadecimal numbers and a string of letters indicating what subscriptions and/or intercepts are active. “Local subscriptions” are what this TTCom client subscribes to from the other client, and “peer subscriptions” are what the other client subscribes to from this TTCom instance. There is now also a section in this guide that lists the subscription and intercept values shown by this command.
  • whoIs also prints user rights, when available, in both hex and word forms. See the User Rights Values section for further information on user rights. Generally, a user can only see the rights applying directly to that user’s current login session; results from whoIs queries for other users will not include user rights.
  • This document includes a TTCom Versus Other TeamTalk Clients section that lists pros and cons of using TTCom.
  • The support for unusually private text messages added and documented in November, 2018 is now documented in its own user guide section and not just in this revision history.
  • The shortening of Facebook ids added in May, 2018 and updated in June, 2018 is removed, as TeamTalk has stopped supporting Facebook-based logins.
  • Added a “Useful Tricks For File Management” section to the documentation for file management commands.
  • Fixed a ResourceWarning under Windows that could occur when a server connection fails.
  • Fixed a small typo in the help text for the url command for creating TeamTalk server links.
  • Custom trigger files work as expected from the precompiled TTCom Windows executable.
  • Finally removed a lot of code for supporting TeamTalk 4 servers.
Revision 1172, March 17, 2021
  • Added file transfer support commands and documentation.
Revision 1146, March 10, 2021

Updates for improved functionality with TeamTalk 5.7:

  • The account list and account delete commands include a -d or --disabled option to list disabled accounts, much like -a or --admin already lists admin accounts. If both admin and disabled accounts are requested at once, only admin accounts will appear.

  • account add allows 0 for a usertype to create a disabled account, and requires confirmation before creating one disabled account from another, just as for creating one admin account from another.

  • account mod allows usertype=0 to change an account to disabled. A typical syntax for disabling an account is account mod Doug usertype=0, and for re-enabling, account mod Doug usertype=1 (or usertype=2 for an admin account).

  • The “neutral” gender for status messages is properly reported, instead of showing up as “on8” and “off8.”

  • Fixed a traceback caused by logins into a 5.7 server with no username under certain not fully determined conditions.

  • Added a bit of code to handle the new support for hidden channels. Other enhancements:

  • The move and kick commands allow multiple-user selection when a user list is presented.

  • The account, ban, and channel commands use a more robust means of handling quotes and argument separation. Arguments that include spaces still need quotes, but some cases where quotes should not have been required but still were should no longer remain.
